title: Protocols, Generics & Opaque Types
scopeHtml: Scope: Protocol-oriented programming, extensions, associated types, generics and constraints, some vs any, existentials, protocol composition, Equatable/Hashable/Codable.

notes.title: Baseline and why protocols are the centre of Swift
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin you model abstraction with interface and abstract class, and generics with <T : Bound>. Swift's equivalent is the protocol, but protocols are more central: structs and enums cannot inherit, so protocols are the only way they share behaviour. Apple calls this "protocol-oriented programming" (WWDC 2015, "Protocol-Oriented Programming in Swift").

Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18. Features gated by version (primary associated types Swift 5.7, some in parameters Swift 5.7, parameter packs Swift 5.9, ~Copyable generics Swift 6) are marked.

Android iOS
interface protocol
default method in interface protocol extension default implementation
abstract class base class or protocol plus extension
generics <T : Comparable<T>> <T: Comparable>
reified / type erasure any Protocol existential or AnyX type-erased wrapper
Parcelable / Serializable Codable
equals/hashCode Equatable / Hashable
data class auto methods synthesised conformance
Comparable Comparable

Everyday analogy. A class hierarchy is a family tree: you inherit from one parent. A protocol is a set of certifications (licensed driver, first-aid trained). Anyone, whatever their family, can hold several certifications.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing protocols as "just interfaces". Extensions, value-type conformance and associated types make them different.
  • Reaching for class inheritance first. Swift reviewers expect protocols plus structs.
  • Assuming every protocol can be used as a plain type; protocols with Self or associated type requirements need some/any or generics.

notes.title: Protocols and protocol extensions with default implementations
notes.html:
Android equivalent. A Kotlin interface can have default method bodies, and you can add extension functions on an interface. In Swift, a protocol declares requirements; an extension on the protocol provides default implementations and extra helper methods.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol Cache {
    associatedtype Value
    func get(_ key: String) -> Value?
}

protocol Describable {
    var name: String { get }
    func describe() -> String          // requirement
}
extension Describable {
    func describe() -> String { "I am \(name)" }     // default implementation
    func shout() -> String { describe().uppercased() }   // extra, NOT a requirement
}

struct Dog: Describable { let name: String }
Dog(name: "Rex").describe()           // uses default
interface Describable {
    val name: String
    fun describe(): String = "I am $name"     // default method
}
fun Describable.shout() = describe().uppercase()   // extension, statically dispatched
class Dog(override val name: String) : Describable

Static vs dynamic dispatch (the classic trap). A method that is a protocol requirement is dispatched dynamically through the witness table: a conforming type's own version wins even when called through the protocol type. A method that exists only in the extension is dispatched statically based on the compile-time type, so a conformer's same-named method is not called when the value is typed as the protocol.

protocol Greeter { func hello() -> String }          // requirement
extension Greeter {
    func hello() -> String { "default hello" }
    func bye() -> String { "default bye" }           // not a requirement
}
struct French: Greeter {
    func hello() -> String { "bonjour" }
    func bye() -> String { "au revoir" }
}
let g: Greeter = French()
g.hello()   // "bonjour"   (witness table)
g.bye()     // "default bye"  (static dispatch to the extension!)

Constrained extensions. Add behaviour only when a condition holds:

extension Collection where Element: Numeric {
    func total() -> Element { reduce(0, +) }          // only for numeric collections
}
extension Describable where Self: Identifiable {
    func tag() -> String { "\(name)#\(id)" }
}

Class-only and inheritance. protocol Delegate: AnyObject restricts to classes (needed for weak). A protocol can inherit others: protocol Pet: Describable, Hashable. @objc protocol with optional requirements is only for Objective-C interop (legacy UIKit delegates).

Retroactive conformance. You can conform an existing type you do not own: extension URL: Identifiable { public var id: String { absoluteString } }. Swift 6 warns when conforming a type from another module to a protocol from yet another module and asks for @retroactive (extension URL: @retroactive Identifiable) to signal the risk of a future duplicate conformance.

Real industry examples. The standard library is built from protocol extensions: map, filter, sorted live on Sequence/Collection extensions, not on concrete types. Alamofire's RequestInterceptor, SwiftUI's View, and Equatable/Hashable/Codable are all protocols with default behaviour. Airbnb and Uber use protocol-based dependency injection so tests can substitute fakes without a mocking framework.

Everyday analogy. A protocol is a job description. The extension is the company handbook with default procedures: you may follow them or do the task your own way, but a procedure that is not in the job description can only be applied if the manager looks at you through the handbook.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting an extension-only method to be overridden by the conformer when called through the protocol type.
  • Forgetting that protocols cannot store properties; default implementations can only use requirements.
  • Using @objc optional in new code; use two protocols or default implementations.
  • Comparing to Kotlin: Kotlin extensions are always static; Swift's requirement methods are dynamic.

notes.title: Associated types and PATs
notes.html:
Android equivalent. A Kotlin generic interface interface Repo<T>. Swift protocols do not take generic parameters in angle brackets; instead they declare associated types, placeholders that each conformer fills in.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol Repository {
    associatedtype Entity
    associatedtype ID: Hashable
    func find(id: ID) async throws -> Entity?
    func save(_ entity: Entity) async throws
}

struct UserRepo: Repository {
    func find(id: Int) async throws -> User? { nil }     // ID and Entity inferred
    func save(_ entity: User) async throws {}
}
interface Repository<Entity, ID> {
    suspend fun find(id: ID): Entity?
    suspend fun save(entity: Entity)
}
class UserRepo : Repository<User, Int> {
    override suspend fun find(id: Int): User? = null
    override suspend fun save(entity: User) {}
}

PAT (Protocol with Associated Types). Such a protocol cannot be used as a bare type in old Swift: let r: Repository was an error ("can only be used as a generic constraint"). The compiler needs to know the associated types to type-check calls. Solutions:

  1. Generic constraint: func load<R: Repository>(from repo: R) where R.ID == Int
  2. Opaque type: func make() -> some Repository
  3. Existential with primary associated types (Swift 5.7+): any Repository<User, Int> if the protocol declares primary associated types: protocol Repository<Entity, ID>.
  4. Type-erased wrapper (legacy): AnyRepository<Entity, ID> holding closures, as in the standard library AnySequence, SwiftUI AnyView, Combine AnyPublisher.
protocol Repository<Entity, ID> {           // primary associated types, Swift 5.7
    associatedtype Entity
    associatedtype ID: Hashable
    func find(id: ID) async throws -> Entity?
}

func show(_ repo: some Repository<User, Int>) async { }       // opaque with constraints
var any: any Repository<User, Int>                            // existential with constraints

Constraining associated types. where Element == String, where C.Element: Equatable. The standard library uses Sequence.Element, Collection.Index, and Sequence.Iterator.

Type erasure pattern (legacy but common in old codebases and interviews).

struct AnyRepository<Entity, ID: Hashable>: Repository {
    private let _find: (ID) async throws -> Entity?
    init<R: Repository>(_ base: R) where R.Entity == Entity, R.ID == ID {
        _find = base.find(id:)
    }
    func find(id: ID) async throws -> Entity? { try await _find(id) }
}

Real industry examples. Combine's Publisher (Output, Failure) is a PAT; AnyPublisher is the erasure that apps return from public APIs. SwiftUI's View has associatedtype Body; that is why you write some View in return types. Swift Composable Architecture's Reducer protocol uses associatedtype State/Action.

Everyday analogy. A protocol with an associated type is a form with a blank: "Container for ___". Each conformer fills in the blank once; you cannot hand someone the blank form and ask them to use it without knowing what goes in it, unless you supply a promise ("a container of User").

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "protocols can't be generic". They have associated types instead of generic parameters.
  • Thinking any P<X> works for any protocol; the protocol must declare primary associated types.
  • Reaching for AnyX wrappers in new code when some/any suffice.
  • Confusing associated types (chosen by the conformer) with generic parameters (chosen by the caller).

notes.title: Generics, where clauses and constraints
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin generics use <T : Bound> and where T : A, T : B, with declaration-site variance (out, in). Swift generics are invariant, resolved at compile time and usually specialised (monomorphised), not erased as on the JVM.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func largest<T: Comparable>(_ items: [T]) -> T? {
    items.max()
}

struct Stack<Element> {
    private var items: [Element] = []
    mutating func push(_ x: Element) { items.append(x) }
    mutating func pop() -> Element? { items.popLast() }
}

func merge<A: Sequence, B: Sequence>(_ a: A, _ b: B) -> [A.Element]
    where A.Element == B.Element, A.Element: Hashable {
    Array(Set(a).union(b))
}
fun <T : Comparable<T>> largest(items: List<T>): T? = items.maxOrNull()

class Stack<E> {
    private val items = mutableListOf<E>()
    fun push(x: E) { items.add(x) }
    fun pop(): E? = items.removeLastOrNull()
}

fun <A, B> merge(a: Iterable<A>, b: Iterable<B>): List<A> where B : A = (a + b).distinct()

Key differences from Kotlin.

  • Specialisation, not erasure. The JVM erases List<String> to List; Swift generates (or can generate) specialised code per concrete type in optimised builds, so there is no boxing and no reified trick needed: you can freely use T.self and MemoryLayout<T>.size.
  • No variance annotations: [Dog] converts to [Animal] implicitly only for built-in collections via special-case rules; your own Box<Dog> is not a Box<Animal>.
  • Extensions with conditions (extension Array where Element == Int) replace many Kotlin extension functions with receiver bounds.
  • Generic where clauses can appear on functions, types and extensions, and on individual members (func sum() -> Element where Element: Numeric).
  • Same-type constraints (==) vs conformance constraints (:).
  • Generic subscripts and generic typealiases exist.
  • Cross-module generic code is only specialised if marked @inlinable and the module exposes the body; otherwise it runs through unspecialised witness-table paths (a library-author concern, e.g. in SPM packages).
extension Array where Element: Equatable {
    func removingDuplicates() -> [Element] {
        var result: [Element] = []
        for x in self where !result.contains(x) { result.append(x) }
        return result
    }
}

Performance. A generic function called with a concrete type in the same module is typically inlined and specialised: zero overhead. A non-specialised generic call passes metadata and witness tables (the same machinery as existentials but without the 40-byte container). Whole-module optimisation (the default for Release) maximises specialisation; @_specialize and @inlinable are advanced tools (verify spelling for underscored attributes before relying on them).

Real industry examples. The Swift standard library (Array<Element>, Dictionary<Key: Hashable, Value>, Result<Success, Failure: Error>), the Swift Collections package from Apple (OrderedDictionary, Deque), and Point-Free's libraries all rely heavily on constrained generics.

Everyday analogy. A generic function is a stamp-making machine. In the JVM world the machine makes one blurry stamp that fits anything (erasure). Swift's machine, when it can, cuts a sharp stamp for each shape it sees.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming Swift generics are erased like Java; they are not, and runtime type checks like T.self work.
  • Expecting covariance for custom generic types.
  • Writing where T == Int when you meant T: BinaryInteger and losing flexibility.
  • Overusing generics when a protocol existential would reduce code size (generic specialisation can bloat binary size).

notes.title: some versus any: opaque and existential types
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin you return an interface type (fun make(): Repository) and callers see only the interface; the concrete type is hidden but the call is virtual. Swift gives you two distinct tools with different cost and capabilities.

some P (opaque) any P (existential)
Concrete type fixed, known to the compiler, hidden from caller can vary at runtime
Dispatch static (inlinable) dynamic via witness table
Storage the concrete type itself 40-byte existential container (inline buffer + metadata + witness table)
Can return different types from branches no, must be one type yes
Works with Self/associated types yes yes since Swift 5.7 (with limits)
Swift version 5.1 (return), 5.7 (parameters) 5.6 requires any keyword in Swift 6 mode (warns in 5.x) 
protocol Shape { func area() -> Double }
struct Circle: Shape { var r: Double; func area() -> Double { .pi * r * r } }
struct Square: Shape { var s: Double; func area() -> Double { s * s } }

func makeShape() -> some Shape { Circle(r: 1) }              // always Circle; caller knows only "a Shape"
// func bad(flag: Bool) -> some Shape { flag ? Circle(r: 1) : Square(s: 1) }   // error: different types

func make(flag: Bool) -> any Shape { flag ? Circle(r: 1) : Square(s: 1) }       // OK, boxed

func total(_ shapes: [any Shape]) -> Double { shapes.map { $0.area() }.reduce(0, +) }   // heterogeneous array
func describe(_ s: some Shape) -> String { "\(s.area())" }       // sugar for generic <S: Shape>

Kotlin comparison. Returning an interface in Kotlin is closest to any. Swift's some has no Kotlin counterpart; the nearest idea is a hidden concrete return type. SwiftUI's var body: some View is the famous use: the real type is a deeply nested generic like VStack<TupleView<(Text, Button<Text>)>>, which SwiftUI diffs efficiently because the type is preserved.

Performance implications.

  • some P/generics: the optimiser can inline and specialise; no allocation for the abstraction.
  • any P: a call goes through the witness table, values larger than 24 bytes are heap-allocated, arrays of any P are 40 bytes per element plus boxes, and existential copying involves retain/release. For tiny hot loops (rendering, parsing) prefer generics. For app-level wiring (a [any Plugin] list) the cost is irrelevant.
  • Swift 6 language mode requires the any keyword for existential types (it was optional in Swift 5; the transition is called "ExistentialAny", verify exact flag status for your Xcode).

Opening existentials. Swift 5.7 allows calling a generic function with an any P value, "opening" the box implicitly: func process<T: Shape>(_ t: T), then process(anyShape) works. You cannot compare two any Equatable values with == directly because Self may differ; use a generic helper or AnyHashable.

Real industry examples. SwiftUI view builders return some View; Apple recommends some by default. Plugin or analytics-sink arrays ([any AnalyticsSink]) use any. Sentry and Firebase wrappers in app architecture use any Logger injected via the environment for testability.

Everyday analogy. some Shape is a sealed gift box whose contents are always the same toy that the shop knows about; you only see "a toy that can be assembled". any Shape is a toy bin where each item may be a different toy, so every time you reach in you must read its instruction card (witness table).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing some and any are interchangeable. some hides a single type; any allows many.
  • Returning different concrete types from a some function.
  • Claiming any is deprecated; it is required for existentials in Swift 6 mode.
  • Saying SwiftUI uses any View. It uses some View, and AnyView is a last-resort type-erased wrapper that disables diffing optimisations.

notes.title: Protocol composition and conditional conformance
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin lets a class implement several interfaces and use where T : A, T : B in generics but has no inline "A and B" type for parameters. Swift writes protocol composition as A & B. Conditional conformance (a generic type conforms only when its parameter does) has no direct Kotlin analogue.

protocol Named { var name: String { get } }
protocol Aged { var age: Int { get } }

func greet(_ p: Named & Aged) { print("\(p.name), \(p.age)") }
func greetAll(_ ps: [any Named & Aged]) { ps.forEach(greet) }

typealias Person = Named & Aged & Codable
func save(_ p: some Person) { }

UIViewController & UITableViewDelegate composes a class and a protocol; at most one class may appear. any Sendable & Codable appears constantly in Swift 6 code.

Conditional conformance (Swift 4.1). A generic type conforms to a protocol only when its type arguments satisfy constraints:

struct Box<T> { var value: T }
extension Box: Equatable where T: Equatable {}              // synthesised
extension Box: Hashable where T: Hashable {}
extension Box: Codable where T: Codable {}
extension Box: Sendable where T: Sendable {}

Box(value: 1) == Box(value: 1)         // OK
// Box(value: { }) == Box(value: { })  // error: closure is not Equatable

That is exactly how Array<Element> is Equatable only when Element: Equatable, and Optional<Wrapped> is Codable only when Wrapped: Codable. Because of conditional conformance the standard collections nest naturally: [[Int]], [String: [Int]] and Set<[Int]> all just work for Hashable.

Gotcha: overlapping conformances. A type can conform to a protocol in only one way; you cannot add Box: Equatable where T: Equatable and Box: Equatable where T == Int simultaneously. Also, for dynamic casting (value as? Equatable) conditional conformances are checked at runtime and can be slower.

Real industry examples. SwiftUI's Optional and Array of views conform to View-ish builders via ViewBuilder; TCA's IdentifiedArray conditionally conforms to Equatable/Sendable. The Swift Collections package relies on conditional conformance for Deque: Equatable where Element: Equatable.

Everyday analogy. Composition is a job ad requiring "driver's licence AND first-aid certificate". Conditional conformance is a club rule: "a team of players is eligible for the cup only if every player is eligible".

Common interview traps.

  • Writing A & B with two classes; only one class constraint is allowed.
  • Expecting Box<T> to be Equatable without declaring the extension (synthesis does not apply to generic wrapper conformance unless declared).
  • Forgetting Sendable conditional conformance when crossing actors in Swift 6.
  • Believing conformance can differ between modules in the same program; it is global and unique.

notes.title: Parameter packs and variadic generics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has vararg of one type and lots of overloads (Function0..Function22, Pair, Triple) to cover multiple types. Swift 5.9 introduced parameter packs (SE-0393) to abstract over an arbitrary number of types.

Verify note. The syntax is stable in Swift 5.9/6 but advanced; confirm details in the current Swift book before writing production code. Many iOS apps never write packs themselves; you consume them via SwiftUI and Apple macros.

// each T is a type in the pack; `repeat` expands per element
func zipAll<each T>(_ values: repeat each T) -> (repeat each T) {
    (repeat each values)
}
let t = zipAll(1, "two", 3.0)       // (Int, String, Double)

func allEqual<each T: Equatable>(_ lhs: (repeat each T), _ rhs: (repeat each T)) -> Bool {
    for (l, r) in repeat (each lhs, each rhs) {       // verify: pack iteration syntax added in Swift 6.0
        if l != r { return false }
    }
    return true
}

Why they exist. Before packs, SwiftUI's TupleView and ViewBuilder.buildBlock had overloads for 1 to 10 views; that is why a VStack historically allowed only 10 children. Packs removed that kind of arity cap in libraries that adopt them (verify which Apple APIs have migrated). Swift Testing's parameterised tests (@Test(arguments: ...)) and macro-generated code also use packs.

Related features. Primary associated types, some/any parameters, and generic integer parameters (InlineArray, Swift 6.2; verify) all belong to the same trend of making generics cheaper and more expressive.

Real industry examples. Point-Free and community libraries (e.g. typed dependency containers, zip over N publishers, tuple-returning async let helpers) use packs to replace 10 hand-written overloads with one function. Apple's Swift Regex builder (RegexBuilder) uses variadic-style generics for capture tuples.

Everyday analogy. Before packs you needed a separate shopping-bag size for 1, 2, 3 ... 10 items. A pack is a bag that stretches to hold however many different items you put in while still remembering each item's type.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing variadic parameters (Int..., all same type, array inside) with parameter packs (different types, preserved).
  • Mentioning packs as a beginner topic; they are an advanced library-author feature.
  • Forgetting the repeat keyword when expanding.
  • Claiming SwiftUI has no child limit without checking (verify).

notes.title: Codable: encoding and decoding
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin uses kotlinx.serialization (@Serializable), Moshi, Gson or Jackson, typically via annotation processing or a compiler plugin. Swift uses Codable (Encodable & Decodable), with the compiler synthesising the conformance when all members are Codable.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct User: Codable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    let id: Int
    let fullName: String
    let email: String?
    let createdAt: Date

    enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey {          // map snake_case / renames
        case id, email
        case fullName = "full_name"
        case createdAt = "created_at"
    }
}

let decoder = JSONDecoder()
decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601
let user = try decoder.decode(User.self, from: data)

let encoder = JSONEncoder()
encoder.outputFormatting = [.prettyPrinted, .sortedKeys]
let json = try encoder.encode(user)
@Serializable
data class User(
    val id: Int,
    @SerialName("full_name") val fullName: String,
    val email: String? = null,
    @SerialName("created_at") val createdAt: String,
)
val user = Json.decodeFromString<User>(text)
val json = Json.encodeToString(user)

Strategy helpers. decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase removes most CodingKeys boilerplate. dateDecodingStrategy supports .iso8601, .secondsSince1970, .formatted(...), .custom. For Data use .base64 (default).

Optionals and defaults. An Optional property decodes if the key is missing or null. A non-optional property with a missing key throws DecodingError.keyNotFound. Kotlin lets you give a default in the constructor; Swift's synthesised init(from:) does not use property defaults, so you write a custom initialiser:

struct Settings: Codable {
    var theme: String
    var retries: Int

    init(from decoder: Decoder) throws {
        let c = try decoder.container(keyedBy: CodingKeys.self)
        theme = try c.decodeIfPresent(String.self, forKey: .theme) ?? "system"
        retries = try c.decodeIfPresent(Int.self, forKey: .retries) ?? 3
    }
}

Enums with associated values. Swift 5.5+ synthesises Codable for enums with payloads, but the JSON shape is Swift-specific ({"success":{"_0":...}}), so for real APIs you hand-write init(from:) with a type discriminator, like kotlinx's @SerialName polymorphism.

Errors to recognise. DecodingError.keyNotFound, .typeMismatch, .valueNotFound, .dataCorrupted; each has a codingPath that names the bad field. In production, log codingPath (never the payload with PII). Backend sending "id": "5" where Swift expects Int is the most common cause of failed decodes.

Performance and concurrency. JSONDecoder is reference type, not guaranteed thread-safe for concurrent configuration changes; create one per use or configure once and then only call decode (Foundation says decoding is safe once configured; verify). Large payloads: decode off the main thread (inside an async function or detached task). Alternatives for hot paths: Foundation's newer JSONDecoder in swift-foundation, swift-extras/IkigaJSON, or protobuf/FlatBuffers.

Real industry examples. Alamofire's responseDecodable, URLSession async code (try JSONDecoder().decode(T.self, from: data)), Firebase's Codable support for Firestore (doc.data(as: User.self)), Apple's SwiftData and UserDefaults property wrappers (@AppStorage with RawRepresentable). Plists use PropertyListEncoder.

Everyday analogy. Codable is a translator who can convert your family-photo album to a standard shipping format and back, as long as every photo has a recognised label (member types are Codable). If one photo is of a unique, unlabelled object (closure) the translator refuses.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting struct default values to apply to missing JSON keys. They do not without a custom init(from:).
  • Forgetting CodingKeys when properties are renamed; a missing case causes a compile error, a wrong one a runtime failure.
  • Decoding dates without setting dateDecodingStrategy (the default is a Double seconds value and fails on ISO strings).
  • Assuming one bad array element is skipped; a single failure fails the whole decode unless you use a lossy wrapper.

notes.title: Equatable, Hashable, Comparable and Identifiable
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin gives equals/hashCode/compareTo and data class generates the first two. Swift splits these into small protocols and synthesises them for structs and enums when all members conform.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct Point: Hashable, Comparable {
    let x: Int
    let y: Int
    static func < (a: Point, b: Point) -> Bool { (a.x, a.y) < (b.x, b.y) }   // tuple comparison
}
Set([Point(x: 1, y: 2), Point(x: 1, y: 2)]).count      // 1
[Point(x: 2, y: 0), Point(x: 1, y: 5)].sorted()
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) : Comparable<Point> {
    override fun compareTo(other: Point) = compareValuesBy(this, other, { it.x }, { it.y })
}
setOf(Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)).size   // 1

The hierarchy. Equatable (==) -> Hashable (adds hash(into:)) ; Comparable requires Equatable and <; Identifiable requires var id: ID where ID: Hashable. CaseIterable gives allCases for enums. RawRepresentable backs raw-value enums.

Synthesis rules.

  • A struct/enum gets Equatable/Hashable for free if declared in the type (or same-file extension) and every stored property conforms.
  • Enums without payloads are Equatable/Hashable automatically.
  • Classes get nothing automatically: write == and hash(into:) yourself, and if you override == you must keep hash(into:) consistent, as with Java.
  • Custom hashing: func hash(into hasher: inout Hasher) { hasher.combine(id) }. Hash values are randomised per process launch (seeded), so never persist hashValue or rely on its stability, and do not depend on Set/Dictionary iteration order (same warning as the JVM, stronger in Swift).

Identifiable in SwiftUI. List(items) and ForEach(items) require Identifiable (or an explicit id: \.keyPath). A stable id is how SwiftUI diffs rows; using UUID() generated inside a computed property (new each access) causes every row to be recreated and breaks animations and scroll position, a classic performance bug. Prefer a stored let id from the backend, or a UUID() assigned once at init.

struct Message: Identifiable, Hashable, Codable {
    let id: UUID                 // stable
    var text: String
    // var id: UUID { UUID() }   // WRONG: new id each time, SwiftUI thinks all rows changed
}

Equality semantics. Equality of two structs is member-wise; for floating point, Double.nan != Double.nan, which breaks reflexivity and can make Set and Dictionary misbehave. AnyHashable is a type-erased wrapper to store mixed hashables (used by NavigationPath).

Real industry examples. Diffable data sources (UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource) require Hashable items. SwiftUI NavigationStack(path:) requires Hashable route types. Apollo iOS and TCA use Equatable state for change detection (@ObservableState, Store skipping updates when state is unchanged).

Everyday analogy. Equatable is "are these two keys the same shape?", Hashable is "give me a locker number for this key", Identifiable is "this key has a serial number engraved". Only the serial number lets the SwiftUI cleaner know the key is the same one it saw yesterday.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting classes to get synthesised Equatable.
  • Writing == without matching hash(into:), so Set lookups fail.
  • Using a randomly generated id that changes on each access in SwiftUI lists.
  • Persisting hashValue across launches (it is randomised per process).

notes.title: Synthesised conformance and a full end-to-end example
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin's data class plus @Serializable plus Hilt-provided interfaces. In Swift the same pieces come from protocol conformances the compiler writes for you, plus protocols for dependency injection.

Which conformances the compiler synthesises (when all members conform). Equatable, Hashable, Comparable (enums only, in declaration order, when no payloads need it, or with associated values hand-written), Codable, CaseIterable (no-payload enums), RawRepresentable (raw-value enums), and Sendable for non-public structs/enums whose members are Sendable. Public types do not get implicit Sendable; declare it.

End-to-end example: a protocol-based, generic, Codable feature.

import Foundation

// 1. Domain model: value type, synthesised Equatable/Hashable/Codable/Identifiable/Sendable
struct Article: Codable, Hashable, Identifiable, Sendable {
    let id: Int
    let title: String
    let publishedAt: Date
}

// 2. Abstraction with associated types and primary associated types
protocol Fetching<Item>: Sendable {
    associatedtype Item: Decodable & Sendable
    func fetch() async throws -> [Item]
}

// 3. Concrete implementation (class would also work; struct is fine because no mutable state)
struct RemoteFetcher<Item: Decodable & Sendable>: Fetching {
    let url: URL
    let session: URLSession = .shared

    func fetch() async throws -> [Item] {
        let (data, response) = try await session.data(from: url)
        guard let http = response as? HTTPURLResponse, (200..<300).contains(http.statusCode) else {
            throw URLError(.badServerResponse)
        }
        let decoder = JSONDecoder()
        decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601
        return try decoder.decode([Item].self, from: data)
    }
}

// 4. Test double without any mocking framework
struct StubFetcher: Fetching {
    var items: [Article]
    func fetch() async throws -> [Article] { items }
}

// 5. Consumer depends on `some`/generic or `any`
@MainActor @Observable
final class ArticlesModel {
    private(set) var articles: [Article] = []
    private let fetcher: any Fetching<Article>           // existential for runtime injection

    init(fetcher: any Fetching<Article>) { self.fetcher = fetcher }

    func load() async {
        do { articles = try await fetcher.fetch() }
        catch { articles = [] }                           // real app: expose an error state
    }
}
Languages: Kotlin
data class Article(val id: Int, val title: String, val publishedAt: String)

interface Fetching<Item> { suspend fun fetch(): List<Item> }

class RemoteFetcher<Item>(private val api: Api, private val type: Class<Item>) : Fetching<Item> {
    override suspend fun fetch(): List<Item> = api.get(type)
}

class ArticlesViewModel(private val fetcher: Fetching<Article>) : ViewModel() {
    var articles by mutableStateOf<List<Article>>(emptyList()); private set
    suspend fun load() { articles = runCatching { fetcher.fetch() }.getOrDefault(emptyList()) }
}

What to notice. Equality, hashing, serialisation and thread-safety markers are one-word conformances. The consumer depends on any Fetching<Article> (Swift 5.7+ primary associated types), which a unit test satisfies with StubFetcher. @Observable is the modern replacement for ObservableObject and @Published, which you will see in older codebases.

Testing it with Swift Testing.

import Testing

@MainActor
@Test func loadPopulatesArticles() async {
    let sample = Article(id: 1, title: "Hi", publishedAt: .now)
    let model = ArticlesModel(fetcher: StubFetcher(items: [sample]))
    await model.load()
    #expect(model.articles == [sample])
}

Real industry examples. This shape (protocol plus value models plus injected fakes) is the common baseline in Airbnb, Uber (Needle DI), and apps using the Factory or swift-dependencies libraries. Point-Free's swift-dependencies replaces hand-rolled protocol stubs with controlled closures.

Everyday analogy. The synthesised conformances are the factory pre-printing barcodes, labels and safety stickers on every product that meets the specs; you only hand-write a label when the product is unusual.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming public types are implicitly Sendable; they must declare it.
  • Using any where some/generics would remove existential overhead in hot paths.
  • Writing mock classes via inheritance instead of protocols and value-type stubs.
  • Forgetting @MainActor on UI-facing models in Swift 6 and then hitting isolation errors.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Protocols replace interfaces and abstract classes; value types can conform, classes inherit single parents, and protocol extensions give default behaviour.
  • Requirements dispatch dynamically; extension-only methods dispatch statically, a classic exam trap.
  • Associated types are placeholders chosen by conformers; PATs need some, any with primary associated types (5.7), generics, or legacy type erasure.
  • Swift generics are specialised, not erased; where clauses, same-type constraints, and conditional extensions replace most Kotlin bounds.
  • some P is one hidden concrete type with static dispatch; any P is a runtime-flexible 40-byte existential; Swift 6 mode expects the any keyword.
  • A & B composes protocols (one class max); conditional conformance makes Box<T>: Equatable where T: Equatable.
  • Parameter packs (each/repeat, Swift 5.9, verify details) abstract over arity; mostly for library authors.
  • Codable synthesises encode/decode; customise with CodingKeys and init(from:); defaults do not apply to missing keys by themselves.
  • Equatable/Hashable/Comparable/Identifiable are synthesised for structs and enums; classes need manual work; stable id matters for SwiftUI.
  • Use protocols plus value-type stubs for testable architecture and Swift Testing for unit tests.
